Overview

The lifecycle

The journey shows eight stages (§1.1.1a). The master counts ten (§1.3): it treats keeping data and deleting it as stages of their own. Management runs alongside every other stage (§1.3).

01

Generation

§2.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Data is created by systems, devices, people or algorithms before any later step can begin, whether or not anyone notices. §2.0

In the journey · Stage 1Watch this stage

Where data is born.

Systems, devices, people and algorithms make data before anything else can happen. The rules come first: what it is for, who agreed, how it is handled — and only what is needed. At Tamsworth Health, it is a bedside monitor.

02

Collection

§3.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Collection selects the generated data that matters and brings it from its sources, such as databases, APIs and files, into the system. §3.0

In the journey · Stage 2Watch this stage

Where data is gathered.

Collection brings in the data that matters, without losing any. Each row is checked as it arrives, and sensitive fields travel encrypted. Tamsworth flags rows in doubt but never changes them. All land in Bronze, its raw copy.

03

Processing

§4.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Processing turns collected data into a usable form: it integrates, cleanses and checks the data so it can be prepared for analysis. §4.0

In the journey · Stage 3Watch this stage

Where data is prepared.

Processing makes collected data trustworthy and usable. Tamsworth cleans, reshapes, joins and trims the three parts from Bronze into one row, then tests it. A row that passes becomes Silver; one that fails waits for a person.

04

Storage

§5.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Storage keeps data accessible, protected and backed up: processed data held for future use, usually in databases or datasets, in places that are scalable and reliable. §5.0

In the journey · Stage 4Watch this stage

Where data is kept.

Storage keeps data accessible, protected and backed up. Tamsworth stores the clean Silver row beside Bronze, its raw copy, locks it and backs it up, then moves it to cheaper places as it ages.

05

Management

§6.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Management keeps data accurate, complete and secure across its whole life. It runs alongside every other stage, not after one. KNIME lists its parts as governance, quality, security, access and retrieval, integration, and archiving and deletion. §6.0, §1.3

In the journey · Stage 5Watch this stage

Part 1 of 2Who may see data, and what it means.

Management runs alongside every stage and keeps data accurate, complete and secure. At Tamsworth Health, the stored Silver row gets a description, rules on who may read it, and a record of every read.

↳

Retention and archival

§10.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are hereTold in Stage 5, part 2

Retention keeps data for a set time to meet legal, administrative, operational and business needs. Archival keeps data that is no longer in daily use but is still needed, safe and apart. Some models, Redpanda among them, count this as a stage of its own; KNIME puts archiving inside management, and so does this journey. §10.0, §1.3, §1.2.7c

In the journey · Stage 5Watch this stage

Part 2 of 2How long data lives.

Management also decides how long data is kept, and when it goes. Tamsworth keeps the Silver row for 7 years, then archives it. It is deleted when its keep-period ends, or when a person asks to be erased.

↳

Deletion

§11.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are hereTold in Stage 5, part 2

Deletion removes data securely so it cannot be recovered, once its retention period has ended. Some models count it as a stage of its own; KNIME puts deletion inside management, and so does this journey. §11.0, §1.3, §1.2.7c

06

Analysis

§7.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Analysis uses tools and techniques to find patterns, trends and connections in data, and turns it into insight for business decisions. §7.0

In the journey · Stage 6Watch this stage

Part 1 of 6Where the data starts to answer.

Analysis turns data into insight with four questions: what happened, why, what may happen, and what to do. Tamsworth Health asks them of its governed Silver rows.

Part 2 of 6What happened.

Descriptive analysis asks what happened. Tamsworth's analysts shape the Silver rows into a Gold table for one question, how long patients waited, and average it by month.

Part 3 of 6Why it happened.

Diagnostic analysis asks why. Tamsworth's analysts split November's wait by clinic, then read what patients wrote in the survey.

Part 4 of 6One definition of every number.

A shared report should carry the definition of every number it shows. At Tamsworth Health, “wait” can be counted two ways, and two reports disagree.

Part 5 of 6What may happen.

Predictive analysis says what may happen. At Tamsworth Health, data scientists train a model on past rows to forecast December's wait.

Part 6 of 6What to do.

Prescriptive analysis recommends the best action. At Tamsworth Health, the forecast misses the goal, so data scientists weigh three options, and a person decides.

07

Visualization

§8.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Visualization shows information in pictures that make data understandable and communicate analysis quickly; serving delivers data to the people, apps and processes that use it. §8.0

In the journey · Stage 7Watch this stage

Part 1 of 5Make the answer visible.

Visualization turns results into pictures that are quick to understand, and delivers them to people who need them. At Tamsworth Health, each of Stage 6’s answers gets a chart.

Part 2 of 5One view for the reader.

A dashboard puts the key numbers in one view for its reader. Data scientists build it, and business analysts present it. Tamsworth’s reads from Gold.

Part 3 of 5Follow any number back.

Every number should trace back to its source. At Tamsworth Health, the operations director follows 34 minutes back to its rows.

Part 4 of 5What the gate protects.

Quality rules are applied as data is processed, not after. Tamsworth charts November twice: with the rows that failed Stage 3’s quality gate, and without them.

Part 5 of 5Keep it current.

Dashboards can be real-time, and alerts fire when a number crosses a limit. Tamsworth sets one on each clinic’s weekly wait.

08

Interpretation

§9.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Interpretation makes sense of the analysis and the pictures, and uses them to make business decisions: people review, conclude, suggest an action and tell the story, and the end of the cycle feeds its beginning. §9.0, §9.1.1, §9.2.1

In the journey · Stage 8Watch this stage

Part 1 of 4Say what it means.

Interpretation turns analysis into decisions: it says what the numbers mean. Tamsworth starts from the Stage 7 dashboard.

Part 2 of 4Weigh the options.

A conclusion leads to a suggested action. Tamsworth weighs three options for December: what each would change, and what it would cost.

Part 3 of 4Tell the story, then decide.

Business analysts present the findings as a story; executives decide. At Tamsworth, the analyst presents to the operations director.

Part 4 of 4Act, then learn.

The final step feeds back into the first. At Tamsworth, the decision is carried out and watched.

Act 2

AI across the lifecycle

You are here

AI can do the routine first round of the work on data, but a person still signs off on anything costly or impossible to undo.

This piece looks at the whole lifecycle at once. It covers three things: how to add AI at scale, what that changes, and where a person still has to decide. One caution first. Every number here is somebody’s claim, and none has been independently checked.

Why the data comes first

AI is only as reliable as the data it learns from. Gartner, quoted in two of the sources, found in February 2025 that 63% of organizations either lack the right data management practices for AI or are not sure they have them.

Plenty of organizations use AI. Far fewer can show that it pays. McKinsey’s 2026 survey, quoted second-hand, found nearly nine in ten using AI regularly somewhere in the business. Only 37% said it had added to their earnings.

When an AI project fails, the cause is usually the data, not the model. The data is incomplete, inconsistent or not trusted. In one vendor’s words: “AI does not fix data problems – it magnifies them.”

Clutter makes it worse. When old, duplicated or trivial content piles up, AI tools are more likely to return answers that are irrelevant or misleading.

So managing the lifecycle is no longer just a way to save on storage. It is the groundwork for security, compliance, governance and AI that people can trust. Governance here means the rules: who owns data, who may see it, and what it means.

And manual work can only grow by adding people. AI-assisted work grows with the data.

How to build it to scale

Start with the foundations, not the automation. An organization that is new to managing its data usually does better to set up its governance first.

Then the catalog. It is the list of what data exists and what it means, and most AI features are built on it.

An organization that already governs its data well does not start over. It extends what it has. The new work is usually in two places: tracing data into AI pipelines and training sets, and naming an owner for each model.

There is no agreed first step. Some sources start with retention rules. Others start with the catalog, with data quality, or with the business goal.

Go in steps, and make each step pass a test before the next one starts. One services firm uses tests like these. The business owner has signed off on the targets. Every kind of AI action has someone to approve it. The audit log shows no AI change that went unreviewed.

Start small. Pick one area, measure it, then add the next. And rebuild the work around what AI can do, rather than bolting AI onto the old process.

Most of the effort is not technical. One rule of thumb, passed on by a vendor, puts about 10% of it in algorithms, 20% in data and infrastructure, and 70% in people, process and governance. Skimp on the 70% and the pilot works but the rollout stalls. A second source divides the rule a little differently.

A one-off clean-up does not hold. The clutter comes back unless the rules keep running.

When buying, trust a trial over a demo. Demos run on tidy data. Judge an AI feature only on the organization’s own data.

Budget for more than the license. There are five costs: the license, the computing, the connectors, the set-up, and the hours people spend checking what AI suggests. A budget that counts only the license runs short.

Two questions are still argued over. One platform, or several tools joined together? Data moved into one place, or queried where it sits?

What it changes in a typical enterprise

The lifecycle turns into a loop. AI does not only use data. It makes more of it: prompts, answers, feedback, test results. All of that flows back in.

The same data turns up in several shapes. It can be a record in a warehouse, an input stored for a model, and a chunk in an AI search index, all at once. A lifecycle that tracks data by where it sits cannot tell that these are the same thing.

Copies made for AI outlive the original. Delete the source, and the copies in indexes, caches and embeddings are still there. Embeddings are data turned into numbers a model can search, and they usually hold private and sensitive details.

The reader is often not a person. Someone looking at a dashboard can spot a wrong chart, or ask a colleague. An AI agent, software that acts on its own, does neither. When the context is missing, it does not stop. It answers anyway.

New kinds of data need rules too. Prompts, outputs, summaries and transcripts each need a decision: how long to keep them, and where.

The work moves. It does not vanish. AI takes the routine first round: sizing up new data, drafting rules, matching records. People keep the definitions, the policies, the approvals and the fixes.

The research has two things to say about jobs. One vendor claims teams can handle more data without adding staff at the same rate. And in McKinsey’s 2026 survey, quoted second-hand, 14% of people at organizations using AI said it had helped shrink the workforce over the past year.

Leaders are automating single stages, not the whole lifecycle. In one trade report they said they “aren’t eager to automate the data lifecycle in its entirety”. Experts quoted in it were not sure the technology would be ready to manage all of it “in five or even 10 years”. Some vendors say the opposite.

To see the effect, measure before starting. Set a baseline, then treat every promised saving as a guess to be tested against it.

Where a person must still decide

The rule of thumb is simple. The more a mistake would cost, and the harder it is to undo, the more a person should be the one to approve it.

One services firm sorts the tasks three ways. AI can do a few alone: sizing up new tables, raising an alert when a load looks wrong, tidying dates and phone numbers.

For others, AI suggests and a person checks: how the fields of a new source line up with existing ones, glossary terms, tags that mark data as sensitive, and close calls on whether two records are the same.

Two things always need a person’s approval: changing who may see data, and deleting or archiving it, with an audit trail.

A suggestion can become automatic, but slowly. First it has to be right for months, with every overrule logged.

The rules stay with people. AI can suggest a rule; a data owner sets it. How long data is kept, and what happens to it afterwards, is for legal, compliance, records and business people to decide.

Deletion is the clearest case. The same firm calls it the one action that cannot be undone. A vendor lists four things that make a deletion defensible: the policy that allowed it, a check that no legal hold applied, the approval, and proof the data is gone from everywhere it lived. A legal hold is an order to keep data.

For every AI system, three answers go on record: who owns the data, who approves each use of it, and who answers when a result is challenged.

Every automated step needs a point where a person checks it. The bigger the risk, the closer the check. AI can be confident and wrong.

Regulated firms say no to unsupervised AI. Sanofi is reported as refusing it for patient data, and AOP Health as not using AI to manage the full lifecycle.

How far AI should act alone is the biggest disagreement in the research. Some vendors describe AI that classifies, archives and deletes with no person involved. Others say archiving and deleting should be “recommend, never automate”. The research does not settle it.

What the research does not show

Nobody in the research has measured the return independently. The savings on offer are all claims. One vendor says up to 60% off storage costs for some customers. One services firm reports a client finding data 57% faster.

No source names the person who signs off on putting an AI system to work. None sets out who is responsible for each AI decision, beyond the three answers above.

And no source shows how a deletion reaches the AI copies. The research says they outlive the source. It gives no way to remove data from embeddings, indexes, caches, training sets or models.
